title: Topographic Maps: Sperry's Eye and Eph Gradients

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: A retinal projection in which neighbouring ganglion cells connect to neighbouring target locations is a {{c1::topographic map}}.
cards.back: The projection preserves spatial order.
cards.quote: neighbouring ganglion cells in the retina connect to neighbouring places in the target
cards.section: The map, and three ways to build it

cards.front: What is the midbrain target of retinal axons called in mammals, and in fish, amphibians and birds?
cards.back: Superior colliculus in mammals; optic tectum in fish, amphibians and birds.
cards.quote: called the optic tectum in fish, amphibians and birds, and the superior colliculus in mammals.
cards.section: The map, and three ways to build it

cards.front: Along the anterior-posterior axis of the chick and mouse retinal map, where do temporal and nasal retinal axons terminate?
cards.back: Temporal retina maps to the anterior target; nasal retina maps to the posterior target.
cards.quote: temporal retina maps to the anterior target, nasal retina to the posterior target.
cards.section: The map, and three ways to build it

cards.front: The region where a growing retinal axon retains its branches is its {{c1::termination zone}}.
cards.quote: where an axon "stops" means where it keeps its branches, its termination zone.
cards.section: The map, and three ways to build it

cards.front: How do individual labels, gradients and neighbours differ as rules for placing retinal axons?
cards.back: Labels match cells to specific sites; gradients supply position-dependent molecular levels; neighbour rules place axons relative to other arriving axons.
cards.quote: Neighbours. Each axon places itself relative to the other retinal axons arriving in the target.
cards.section: The map, and three ways to build it

cards.front: After a rotated adult newt eye regained vision following optic nerve regrowth, aiming errors persisted. What wiring idea did this argue against?
cards.back: Random wiring subsequently matched to useful function by experience: repeated errors did not correct the rotated responses.
cards.quote: The result argued against random wiring matched by use.
cards.section: Sperry's newts: does the wiring follow the eye or the world?

cards.front: In an eye-rotation study, compare leaving the optic nerve intact with cutting it and allowing regeneration. Which condition tests target selection anew, and why?
cards.back: Cutting and regrowth: axons must choose targets again. An intact nerve preserves old connections, so persistent aiming errors alone do not test reconnection.
cards.quote: since the old connections were never broken.
cards.section: Sperry's newts: does the wiring follow the eye or the world?

cards.front: What did the chemoaffinity hypothesis propose about retinal cells and their targets?
cards.back: Cells acquire position-dependent chemical differences, and targets carry matching differences. Crossing gradients could specify coordinates without a unique label for every cell.
cards.quote: Sperry proposed that retinal cells acquire chemical differences according to their position and that their targets carry matching differences.
cards.section: Sperry's newts: does the wiring follow the eye or the world?

cards.front: A rotated eye recovers vision after nerve regeneration but retains rotated aiming errors. Does this establish a particular chemical guidance mechanism? Explain the inferential limit.
cards.back: No. The behaviour supports position-specific reconnection, but does not identify a molecule or uniquely establish chemical matching. The rule is that a functional outcome can constrain wiring without proving its molecular cause.
cards.quote: The behaviour supported position-specific reconnection without proving a molecular mechanism
cards.section: Sperry's newts: does the wiring follow the eye or the world?

cards.front: In the chick stripe assay, heating only posterior tectal membranes removed temporal axons’ avoidance. What did this indicate about the guidance cue?
cards.back: A heat-sensitive repellent on posterior membranes. An anterior attractant should still have favoured the unheated anterior lanes.
cards.quote: Heating the posterior membranes abolished the temporal axons' avoidance.
cards.section: Is the cue in the target? The stripe assay

cards.front: Temporal chick retinal axons avoid posterior membrane when offered alternating anterior/posterior lanes. They grow well on either membrane alone. What alternative explanation does the single-membrane control weaken?
cards.back: That posterior membrane is simply a poor growth surface. Growth on it alone shows that the preference emerges when axons can choose.
cards.quote: The last row matters: posterior membrane was not simply a poor surface.
cards.section: Is the cue in the target? The stripe assay

cards.front: In a retinal stripe assay, suppose preference depends solely on a heat-sensitive attractant on anterior lanes. Only those lanes are heated; posterior lanes remain intact. What happens to preference, and why?
cards.back: Anterior preference disappears, because heating removes the assumed anterior attractant. This follows the assay’s logic of selectively disabling the membrane carrying the proposed cue.
cards.quote: An attractant on the anterior lanes, which were not heated, would have kept the preference.
cards.section: Is the cue in the target? The stripe assay

cards.front: Eph receptors belong to the {{c1::receptor tyrosine kinase}} family.
cards.quote: Eph receptors are the largest family of receptor tyrosine kinases
cards.section: The molecules: two opposite slopes

cards.front: In the chick retinal projection, which ends of the retina and tectum have the highest EphA3 receptor and ephrin-A2 ligand levels, respectively?
cards.back: EphA3 is highest in temporal retina; ephrin-A2 is highest in posterior tectum.
cards.quote: high in temporal ganglion cells and low in nasal ones.
cards.section: The molecules: two opposite slopes

cards.front: Ephrin-A ligands are attached to the outer cell surface by a {{c1::GPI anchor}}.
cards.back: A lipid tail holds them at the surface.
cards.quote: Ephrin-As are held to the outer surface by a GPI anchor (a lipid tail)
cards.section: The molecules: two opposite slopes

cards.front: What do forward and reverse signalling mean for an Eph receptor–ephrin pair?
cards.back: Forward signalling enters the receptor-bearing cell; reverse signalling enters the ephrin-bearing cell.
cards.quote: the receptor signals forward into its own cell, and the ephrin can signal in reverse into the cell that carries it
cards.section: The molecules: two opposite slopes

cards.front: A receptor and its ligand both remain tethered to opposing cell surfaces. The cells are kept physically apart. What happens to their direct signalling, and why?
cards.back: Direct signalling cannot occur, because the surface-bound partners cannot contact each other. The rule is that this interaction requires cell-surface contact.
cards.quote: Because both partners sit on cell surfaces, signalling needs contact
cards.section: The molecules: two opposite slopes

cards.front: Why does a retinal axon with more EphA end farther anteriorly in the fixed-threshold toy model?
cards.back: More receptor reaches the same receptor × ligand limit at a lower ephrin-A level, which occurs farther anteriorly.
cards.quote: The axon with the most receptor reaches the limit soonest
cards.section: Why more receptor means less ligand

cards.front: In the toy retinal map, repulsion is R × L and the branch limit is 3. Ligand L rises linearly from 1 anteriorly to 3 posteriorly. For R = 2.5 units, where is the termination zone?
cards.back: L = 3/2.5 = 1.2 units. Fraction of the target axis = (1.2 − 1)/(3 − 1) = 0.10: 10% back from the anterior edge.
cards.quote: It keeps its branches where that product reaches a limit of 3.
cards.section: Why more receptor means less ligand

cards.front: In the fixed-threshold retinal toy, R = 3 and R × L must reach 3. Normally L(x) = 1 + 2x, with x = 0 anterior and 1 posterior. Halve target ligand everywhere. Where does this axon end?
cards.back: After halving, L(x) = 0.5 + x. Solve 3(0.5 + x) = 3: x = 0.5, halfway back, instead of the original x = 0.
cards.quote: Ephrin-A rises in a straight line from 1 at the front edge of the target to 3 at the back edge.
cards.section: Why more receptor means less ligand

cards.front: Why is the EphA × ephrin-A branch limit not a wall that stops a chick or mouse retinal growth cone?
cards.back: The axon overshoots. Ephrin-A limits where branches form and survive; the overshooting axon segment is later removed.
cards.quote: the "limit" is where branches can survive, not a wall the growth cone hits.
cards.section: Why more receptor means less ligand

cards.front: What positional question does repulsion alone leave unanswered in the retinal fixed-threshold toy?
cards.back: It sets the farthest posterior branching limit, but does not explain why an axon avoids branching farther anteriorly. A counterforce or axon comparison is needed.
cards.quote: a repellent alone says only how far back an axon may branch, not why it does not branch further forward.
cards.section: Why more receptor means less ligand

cards.front: An axon termination zone located in the wrong place is described as {{c1::ectopic}}.
cards.quote: Termination zones are ectopic (in the wrong place) and multiple
cards.section: Is the slope needed? Ephrin knockouts

cards.front: What does the progressively worse mapping defect as ephrin-A2/A5 dosage falls in mice show about ligand information?
cards.back: Ligand amount carries positional information. Axons still reach the colliculus, but reduced ligand produces increasingly inaccurate and multiple termination zones.
cards.quote: The defect grows as ligand is lowered, which says that the amount of ephrin, not merely its presence, carries position.
cards.section: Is the slope needed? Ephrin knockouts

cards.front: A guidance-ligand knockout removes the ligand from both projecting neurons and their target. How could you test whether target ligand specifically accounts for the mapping defect?
cards.back: Compare target-only removal with neuron-only removal, tracing the same retinal region in each and in controls. The rule is that removing ligand from both sites cannot localise its causal contribution.
cards.quote: One caveat: the knockout removed the ephrins from the retina as well as the target.
cards.section: Is the slope needed? Ephrin knockouts

cards.front: Placing a chosen coding sequence within a gene so it is expressed wherever that gene is active is a {{c1::knock-in}}.
cards.quote: a knock-in, which places a chosen coding sequence in a gene so it is made wherever that gene is on
cards.section: Absolute or relative? Two maps from one retina

cards.front: How do fixed-threshold and pure-rank models differ in assigning a retinal axon’s target position?
cards.back: Fixed threshold uses its own receptor level and local ligand. Pure rank uses its signal relative to other axons, with target space allocated by rank.
cards.quote: Each axon's place depends on how its EphA signal compares with the other axons'.
cards.section: Absolute or relative? Two maps from one retina

cards.front: In a continuous pure-rank retinal toy, baseline EphA = 1 + 2t, with uniform cell density for t = 0 nasal to 1 temporal. Exactly half at every t gain 4 units. Highest rank maps to 0% anterior, lowest to 100% posterior. Where does an unchanged t = 0.5 axon map?
cards.back: All changed axons (5–7 units) outrank it: 50% of all cells. Half the unchanged cells also outrank it: 0.5 × 50% = 25%. Total ahead = 75%, so it ends 75% back.
cards.quote: The axon with the most signal takes the front of the target, the next takes the space behind it
cards.section: Absolute or relative? Two maps from one retina

cards.front: In the retinal toy, half the axons at each retinal position have EphA levels of 5–7; the rest have 1–3. Target ephrin-A rises from 1 to 3; the fixed product limit is 3. What happens to the extra-receptor population under fixed-threshold versus evenly spaced pure-rank rules, and why?
cards.back: Fixed threshold crowds them at the anterior edge: even the lowest target ligand produces above-limit repulsion. Pure rank gives them an ordered map across the anterior half: they comprise half the axons and all outrank the unchanged population.
cards.quote: The axon with the most signal takes the front of the target, the next takes the space behind it
cards.section: Absolute or relative? Two maps from one retina

cards.front: In mice with two copies of the Isl2-EphA3 knock-in, unchanged retinal axons occupy the posterior half of the colliculus while extra-receptor axons occupy the anterior half. Why do the unchanged axons challenge an absolute receptor address?
cards.back: They changed position despite retaining their own receptor levels. Their endings therefore depend on other axons, which a fixed address in their own receptor level cannot explain.
cards.quote: nothing about them was altered, yet they ended somewhere new, which a purely absolute reading cannot explain.
cards.section: Absolute or relative? Two maps from one retina

cards.front: Combine the Isl2-EphA3 displacement of unchanged axons with mapping defects after ephrin-A dosage reduction. What must an adequate model of these mouse retinal-mapping results include?
cards.back: Both comparison among axons and ligand amount. Unchanged-axon displacement rules out a fixed receptor address; ligand-dosage effects rule out pure rank alone. The governing rule is rank set against a ligand slope.
cards.quote: The knock-in rules out a fixed address in the axon's own receptor level; the dosage result rules out pure rank.
cards.section: Absolute or relative? Two maps from one retina

cards.front: Every retinal ganglion cell receives the same positive EphA increment, leaving target ligand unchanged. Under fixed-threshold versus pure-rank rules, what happens and why?
cards.back: Fixed threshold shifts endings anteriorly, clipping any out-of-range positions to the front edge, because less ligand is needed. Pure rank preserves the map because adding the same amount preserves every rank.
cards.quote: Pure rank: nothing moves, because no axon's rank has changed.
cards.section: Absolute or relative? Two maps from one retina

cards.front: After coarse retinal targeting, termination zones are sharpened by {{c1::correlated spontaneous activity}} in the retina.
cards.quote: Correlated spontaneous activity in the retina then sharpens them.
cards.section: Where slopes stop being enough

cards.front: How do molecular guidance and correlated retinal activity contribute differently to a topographic map?
cards.back: Molecular cues establish coarse positions; correlated activity sharpens broad termination zones. Their actions overlap in time and interact.
cards.quote: Chemistry lays out the map and activity sharpens it, though the two act at overlapping times and interact
cards.section: Where slopes stop being enough

cards.front: Suppose molecular guidance is preserved but correlated retinal activity is disrupted during map refinement. What happens to coarse targeting and termination-zone size, and why?
cards.back: Axons should reach roughly the right regions but retain broad, diffuse zones: molecular cues provide coarse targeting, while correlated activity sharpens the branches.
cards.quote: axons reach roughly the right region but their termination zones stay large and diffuse
cards.section: Where slopes stop being enough

cards.front: A model assigns retinal map layout entirely to molecular gradients and allows activity only to sharpen it afterward. Which EphA3 knock-in observation challenges that separation?
cards.back: Retinal waves help determine how the two maps are organised. The lesson’s rule is that molecular guidance and activity overlap and interact, so activity cannot be restricted to a separate final sharpening step.
cards.quote: in the EphA3 knock-in mice, retinal waves help decide how the two maps are organised.
cards.section: Where slopes stop being enough

cards.front: In a receptor-ratio retinal toy, compare neighbours with levels 1 and 1.1 units versus 2.9 and 3 units. Add 1 unit to every cell. Calculate each higher/lower ratio before and after; where is the percentage difference reduced more?
cards.back: Nasal pair: 1.1/1 = 1.10 → 2.1/2 = 1.05 (10% → 5%). Temporal pair: 3/2.9 ≈ 1.0345 → 4/3.9 ≈ 1.0256 (3.45% → 2.56%). Reduction is larger nasally: 5 versus about 0.88 percentage points. The ratio rule permits changed spacing despite preserved order; actual spacing needs a position rule.
cards.quote: a fixed increment shrinks the ratio between neighbours most where EphA is low.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A retinal toy with uniform cell density adds 1 EphA unit to half the cells at each position. A ratio rule distinguishes populations only above 1.5. Design a nasal-versus-temporal tracing comparison with pure rank, assuming baseline EphA rises linearly from 1 to 3.
cards.back: Trace changed and unchanged axons separately at both poles. Ratios are 2/1 = 2 nasally and 4/3 ≈ 1.33 temporally, so the invented ratio threshold separates only nasal populations. Pure rank predicts equal changed–unchanged rank separations at the two poles. The rule compares signal ratios versus counts of intervening axons; physical spacing needs another rule.
cards.quote: Under pure rank, separation depends only on how many axons have levels between the two populations
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How does the direction of the EphB/ephrin-B gradients differ from the EphA/ephrin-A pairing in the retinal map?
cards.back: High ventral EphB pairs with high medial ephrin-B. By contrast, high temporal EphA maps toward low anterior ephrin-A; other cues also help organise the second axis.
cards.quote: EphB receptors, high in ventral retina, and ephrin-B ligands, high in the medial target, help sort axons along it
cards.section: The other axis

cards.front: Suppose retinal axons move only away from the posterior-high ephrin-A repellent, with no counterforce or stabilising placement rule. What happens to the map, and why?
cards.back: Axons pile up anteriorly rather than spreading across the target. Repulsion alone favours moving toward lower ligand; a counterforce is needed to support distributed positions.
cards.quote: Without some counterforce, axons that simply moved away from a repellent would all pile up at the front.
cards.section: How might axons compare themselves?
